title: The night prayer
hook: prayer after sleeping and waking in the night

segments.voice: Yesterday, witr, the odd prayer, and your line: end the night odd. How did last night end, with an odd unit of prayer or with one quiet moment? Today we stay in the night. Day one thousand eighty-two.

A quarter past three in the morning. The house is dark, the phone is face-down, the fridge is humming to itself. Someone gets out of a warm bed, and not because a baby cried or a dream went wrong. On purpose. Cold water on the hands and face for wudu. A mat unrolled in the corner of the bedroom. No adhan calls this prayer. Nobody at the mosque will notice who came. The street outside is asleep, and that is part of the point. It's a prayer you go to sleep before, and then get up for. Today's word is the prayer that begins with waking.
screen: `A QUARTER PAST THREE.` → `UP ON PURPOSE.` → `NO ADHAN CALLS THIS ONE.`

segments.voice: Tahajjud is the voluntary prayer of the night, prayed after you've slept and woken. First, the Qur'an, where it begins as words addressed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself. Pickthall's translation of surah seventeen gives them: "And some part of the night awake for it, a largess for thee." A largess: something extra, a gift beyond what was owed. That's the shape of tahajjud. The five daily prayers are the duty. This one is the gift on top. Second, the people the Qur'an describes. In surah thirty-two, Pickthall has them as those "Who forsake their beds to cry unto their Lord in fear and hope." Forsake their beds. It's an honest picture. The bed is warm, and leaving it costs something. Third, why the dark hours. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that every night, when its last third remains, God asks: who is calling on Me, so that I may answer? Who is asking, so that I may give? Who seeks forgiveness, so that I may forgive? Some readers hear the timing as an invitation: the quietest hour is the one the hadith describes as open. Fourth, what it looked like in one life. Aisha, his wife, saw the Prophet stand in the night prayer until his feet swelled. She asked why he did this, when he had already been forgiven. He answered with a question: should I not be a grateful servant? In that answer, the night prayer isn't a debt being paid down. It's thanks. And it sits right beside yesterday's word. The hadith asks that witr be the last of the night's prayer, so when both are prayed, tahajjud comes first and the night still closes odd. Some keep the night prayer often, some in hard seasons, some in Ramadan, some rarely. The gift is described the same way for all of them.
screen: `A LARGESS: THE GIFT ON TOP.` · `THEY FORSAKE THEIR BEDS.` · `WHO IS CALLING ON ME?` · `SHOULD I NOT BE GRATEFUL?` · then, large: `AND SOME PART OF THE NIGHT AWAKE FOR IT.`

segments.voice: The practice is two units in the night. For now, settle, and let your breath slow. Choose one night this week when you might wake, and see it clearly: the dark room, the cold water, the corner where you'd stand. If you pray, you can set your intention now to rise after sleeping and pray two units. If you don't, you can set an alarm a few minutes early and spend those minutes awake and quiet, before the day gets a say. For now, sit in the quiet as if it were that hour. The bell holds the time.
Tahajjud. The voluntary night prayer, prayed after sleeping and waking, a gift beyond the duty. Today's word.
Your line: awake for him. Tonight, if you wake for any reason, leave the phone where it is. Give the first minute of being awake to quiet, or to prayer. Day one thousand eighty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims who keep tahajjud usually sleep first, then rise in the later part of the night, make wudu and pray voluntary units in pairs, often finishing with witr before the dawn prayer.

fork.setup: you're Aisha. night after night you watch the Prophet stand in prayer until his feet swell, though he has already been forgiven. what do you do?
options: say nothing and go back to sleep.
ask him why he does it.
fork.reveal: she asked, and he answered with a question of his own: should I not be a grateful servant? (Sahih al-Bukhari 4837)

original.note: Arabic: the night vigil. the verb form appears in Qur'an 17:79.

trapdoor: what you thought: staying up late to pray.
what it means: a voluntary prayer after you've slept and woken, the gift on top of the five.
what a scholar hears: 17:79 commands the vigil with the verb itself and calls it nafilah, something extra, the same word used for voluntary prayer.

notes: Editor: added the missing 'First' so the teach's steps read in order; Bukhari 1145 timing given as the hadith's 'last third' of the night; 'Muslims hear the timing' softened to 'some readers'; the unsourced 'witr is often prayed last' replaced with the hadith's instruction (Bukhari 998, day 1081).
Pickthall 17:79 and 32:16 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording and punctuation (Pickthall 17:79 continues 'It may be that thy Lord will raise thee (O Muhammad) to a praised estate').
Trapdoor: 17:79 reads 'fa-tahajjad bihi nafilatan laka'. Confirm that tahajjud and nafilah are stated accurately.
Bukhari 1145 (the divine descent in the last third of the night) is paraphrased without the descent wording and with 'the last part of every night'; Keeper may prefer the hadith's own phrasing.
Bukhari 4837 (Aisha and the swollen feet) paraphrased.
'Witr is often prayed last, after tahajjud' follows the hadith instruction to make witr the last night prayer; confirm phrasing.
Previous days 1072–1081 were not on disk when this was written; the review uses the index for day 1081 (witr, 'end the night odd').
